cases.title: Sukulu phosphate project: land signed over for 99 years and no titles issued
cases.place: Sukulu village, Osukuru and Rubongi sub-counties, Tororo District, Uganda
cases.point: Sukulu village, Tororo District (OpenStreetMap village node, through Nominatim). AidData's record 60236 gives approximate coordinates of 0.623611, 34.153611 for the plant site, about 11 km outside Tororo town. The land complaints are reported across Osukuru and Rubongi sub-counties, so this point is an area, not the parcels taken.

lenders.name: Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC)
lenders.role: AidData record 60236. A US$240 million project financing facility signed on 4 December 2015 with Guangzhou Dong Song Energy Group (U) Co., Limited, the company developing the site, with credit insurance from Sinosure. The proceeds were to part-finance a commercial contract with 23rd Metallurgical Construction Group Company Limited. AidData records that in 2019 ICBC told the company it was withholding US$60 million, at least part of it the undisbursed balance of the loan, and that some sources put the full facility for the whole project at up to US$520 million. This is not a World Bank project and has no P-number.

cases.conditions: The credit went to the Chinese developer rather than to the Ugandan state, and its proceeds were to pay a Chinese contractor, 23rd Metallurgical Construction Group Company Limited (AidData record 60236). The Tororo District Council and the Government of Uganda accepted the company's application on condition that it compensate all persons living on the land and evict no one; Matooke Republic reported on 16 December 2016 that the company had defaulted on that condition.

companies.name: Guangzhou Dong Song Energy Group (U) Co., Limited
companies.role: Borrower and developer; held the exploration licence granted on 1 August 2013 and took the land under surface rights agreements (AidData record 60236; Oil in Uganda, 8 July 2016)
companies.desc: Ugandan subsidiary of a Guangzhou energy and minerals group, set up to build the Osukuru industrial complex: a phosphate fertiliser plant, a sulphuric acid plant, a steel mill, a rare earth plant and a 12 MW thermal power station (AidData record 60236).

companies.name: 23rd Metallurgical Construction Group Company Limited
companies.role: Contractor for the works the ICBC credit financed (AidData record 60236)

companies.name: ABMAK Associates
companies.role: Ugandan law firm that handled the land transactions for the company and defended the payments made (CorpWatch, 8 July 2016)

cases.community: Guangzhou Dong Song Energy was awarded 26.5 square kilometres, and the development could displace as many as 12,000 people in 14 villages; the community dropped its opposition in exchange for land titles, and the company's lawyers said villagers were paid 30 million shillings (US$8,750) an acre for a 99-year lease (CorpWatch, 8 July 2016). Rose Tibita, one of hundreds of residents affected in Osukuru and Rubongi sub-counties, said: "When I went in, they opened for me pieces of paper and said you sign here. I first hesitated and asked where the rest of the (project affected) people were, they told me if I don't want the money, I should get out, and if I don't sign my land would be taken by government for free." Vincent Matano said: "To my surprise, they have taken our money, our land and no land title has been given to any of us." The company's lawyer Denis Kusasira said people had been told they could take money or be resettled and none chose resettlement, that the rate was 30 million shillings an acre plus payment for crops and other developments and a 30 per cent disturbance allowance, and that "We are not one hundred percent clean, but this ... should be a case study". Henry Okwalanga said he had benefited and that the company built him a house in place of a grass-thatched hut (CorpWatch; Oil in Uganda, 8 July 2016, as summarised by the Business and Human Rights Resource Centre). On 16 December 2016 Matooke Republic reported that over 4,600 families had waited more than a year for payment and that only 123 of 4,800 families had received any compensation payment; it gives both figures. Jackson Oryema said: "I don't believe that I can be treated like this in my own country and my own government can allow this it is very unfair and we should be compensated." Some families said they were made to sign 99-year leases instead of the 21 years agreed, and that spousal consent rules were not followed and some forms were pre-signed. A district official said compensation should have been done by August 2014 and that two years of inflation had cut the value of the money. The Tororo district chairperson Emmanuel Osuna said landowners should be paid at government approved rates. The Resident District Commissioner Martin Orochi said the claims were untrue, that people who complained were using the land for perennial agriculture and did not own it so were not entitled to compensation, that they had agreed to leave after their crops matured and were going peacefully, and that anyone complaining was "just a fraudster" (Matooke Republic).
cases.displaced_note: No document counting people or households actually moved was found. CorpWatch's figure of as many as 12,000 people in 14 villages is the reach of the awarded area, not a count of people moved. Matooke Republic's figures count families awaiting payment: 123 of 4,800 paid as of 16 December 2016, in an article that also says over 4,600 families.
cases.outcome: The fertiliser plant was commissioned on 24 October 2018 and produced 50,000 tonnes of bio-organic fertiliser for a trial season. Commercial production was then halted by a legal dispute over the mineral deposit that led to the cancellation of the company's mining lease, and ICBC withheld disbursements (AidData record 60236). No later record was found of land titles being issued to the families who signed the surface rights agreements.

cases.confidence_note: The land complaints come from three sources outside the lender: a Ugandan reporter for Oil in Uganda, a Ugandan weekly and CorpWatch, with the company's lawyers answering in two of them. The compensation rate of 30 million shillings an acre is the company's lawyers' own figure. One article gives two totals for the families involved, over 4,600 and 4,800, and does not explain the gap. The Resident District Commissioner denies the claims and says those complaining did not own the land. Oil in Uganda's own page was reached only through the Business and Human Rights Resource Centre's summary of it.
cx: Sukulu phosphate land leases and unpaid compensation
cases.ecosystem: The deposit is the Sukulu carbonatite complex, surveyed in 2008 at an estimated 206 million tonnes of minerals, and the company was awarded 26.5 square kilometres of it for phosphate and rare earths (CorpWatch, 8 July 2016).
cases.whole: The company said the complex would create at least 1,000 jobs and produce 300,000 tonnes of phosphate fertiliser and 300,000 tonnes of steel a year, with revenue of about 1.6 trillion Ugandan shillings a year (CorpWatch, 8 July 2016). The plant produced one trial batch of 50,000 tonnes of bio-organic fertiliser after commissioning in October 2018 and then stopped (AidData record 60236). No independent production figure was found.

cases.title: SGR Phase 1 at Miritini: land acquired and four allottees left without land or payment
cases.point: Miritini, Jomvu sub-county, Mombasa (OpenStreetMap suburb, through Nominatim). The land is part of plot MN/VI/4805 and the parcels in dispute are numbers 3912 and 3913/VI/MN; the court records give no coordinate, so the point is the suburb.

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: AidData records 37103 and 31777. Two loan agreements signed with Kenya's National Treasury on 11 May 2014 for Phase 1 of the Standard Gauge Railway: a buyer's credit of US$2,003,584,028.87, later revised to US$1,903,404,827.42, at 6-month Libor plus 3.6 per cent with a 15.25-year maturity and insurance from Sinosure; and a preferential buyer's credit of US$1.6 billion at 2 per cent with a 20.25-year maturity. The proceeds were on-lent to Kenya Railways Corporation to pay 90 per cent of two contracts with China Road and Bridge Corporation. This is not a World Bank project and has no P-number.

cases.conditions: Repayment was secured on project revenue held in escrow, with minimum balances set by a 2014 escrow account agreement, and on a take-or-pay freight agreement under which the Kenya Ports Authority had to consign a minimum volume of cargo to the railway or make good the shortfall; a 1.5 per cent Railway Development Levy on imports was set up to cover any gap and the government's own share of the cost. The loans financed 90 per cent of the two commercial contracts with China Road and Bridge Corporation, with the remaining 10 per cent paid by Kenya Railways (AidData records 37103 and 31777). Land acquisition and compensation were the Kenyan state's responsibility, carried out by the National Land Commission.

companies.name: National Land Commission
companies.role: The Kenyan state body that compulsorily acquired the land and refused to pay the four allottees (Court of Appeal, Civil Application 10 of 2020)
companies.desc: Independent commission created by Kenya's 2010 constitution to manage public land on behalf of the national and county governments and to carry out compulsory acquisition and pay compensation under the Land Act.

companies.name: China Road and Bridge Corporation
companies.role: Builder of the Mombasa-Nairobi line under the two contracts the loans financed (AidData record 37103)

companies.name: Kenya Railways Corporation
companies.role: State railway that borrowed the proceeds and supervised the works (AidData record 37103)

companies.name: Miritini Free Port Limited
companies.role: Registered owner of the plot, which received the compensation for the acquisition (Court of Appeal, Civil Application 10 of 2020)

cases.community: The National Land Commission compulsorily acquired 22.11 hectares of plot MN/VI/4805 for the Mombasa-Nairobi Standard Gauge Railway and paid Kshs 1,475,486,845 to Miritini Free Port Limited, the registered owner. Theresia Runji, Marieta Gitonga Chege, Naomi Kiio and Sammy M. Kara, who had been issued letters of allotment for part of the same land in 2000, then filed Mombasa Constitutional Petition No. 17 of 2018, and the commission denied their claim (Court of Appeal ruling in Civil Application 10 of 2020, 20 November 2020, as published by judy.legal). The High Court held that the commission had abused its statutory powers in refusing to compensate the four, that the decision was unconstitutional because they were never heard, and that they had not been served with notice of the government's intention to acquire the land. Justice Eric Ogola directed the commission to value and pay for parcels 3912 and 3913/VI/MN as at the date of acquisition plus interest at commercial rates, and said: "My understanding is that this money has already been disbursed and the petitioners left without land. Justice demands that the petitioners be justly and promptly compensated for the loss of their land." He also held they were entitled to damages. Their lawyer Gikandi Ngibuini argued their right to prompt and full compensation had been infringed, exposing them to economic hardships, losses and damages, and their petition said the allotment had followed an earlier eviction from parcels at Bombolulu. The commission argued they had produced no evidence that the land was subject to compulsory acquisition; Miritini Free Port called the petition an abuse of court process; the judge noted unchallenged evidence that Miritini Free Port remained the registered owner of the undisputed part of the land, and said the judgment covered only the two parcels claimed (Daily Nation, 2 December 2019).
cases.displaced_note: No document counting people moved for this section was found. The court records four allottees left without the land and without payment.
cases.outcome: The railway was completed on 31 May 2017 (AidData record 37103). After the High Court ruling the commission went to the Court of Appeal, which heard the matter as Civil Application 10 of 2020 and ruled on 20 November 2020; no public record of the result of that application, or of payment to the four, was found.

cases.confidence_note: The harm sits in a court record and in a Kenyan newspaper's report of the judgment, both outside the lender. The two sources name the petitioners differently: the court record gives Theresia Runji, Marieta Gitonga Chege, Naomi Kiio and Sammy M. Kara, and the Daily Nation gives Theresa Runji, Marieta Gitonga, Naomi Kiio and Sammy Macharia. The two also differ on the money paid to the registered owner: the court record gives Kshs 1,475,486,845 and the Daily Nation gives Sh1.4 billion and another Sh360,000. Only the opening of the Court of Appeal ruling is published without a subscription, so the result of that application is not carried here. The High Court judgment itself was not opened; its contents here come from the newspaper's report and from the Court of Appeal ruling's account of the case.
cx: Standard Gauge Railway Phase 1 land acquisition at Miritini
cases.whole: The 485 km line from Mombasa to Nairobi opened on 31 May 2017, eighteen months ahead of schedule, and was the largest infrastructure project built in Kenya since independence. A report by Kenya's transport ministry tabled in parliament in 2018 said the railway lost KES 9.8 billion (US$90.3 million) in its first year; a 2020 ministry report said it lost US$200 million over three years, on revenue of US$230.7 million against operating costs of US$430.5 million. In July 2022 Kenya received overdue repayment notices from China Eximbank, and local media reported a default and a default interest charge of US$10.8 million (AidData record 37103).

cases.title: Kibwezi-Mutomo-Kitui road: land and shops taken and compensation unpaid since 2017
cases.place: Kitui town and the Kibwezi-Migwani road, Kitui and Makueni Counties, Kenya
cases.point: Kitui town, where those affected gathered at the county commissioner's office in December 2020 and March 2022 (OpenStreetMap city node, through Nominatim). The road runs about 172 km from Kibwezi to Migwani through Mutomo, Kitui and Kabati, so this point is one place along it.

lenders.name: China Eximbank
lenders.role: AidData records 53111 and 58152. A buyer's credit agreement signed with the Government of Kenya on 29 November 2016 covering 85 per cent of commercial contracts worth KES 50 billion for three sections totalling 472 km; AidData estimates the face value at US$418,578,082.97 and records no official figure for it. Phase 1, 192 km worth KES 23 billion, is recorded separately as record 58152 at US$194.7 million. Terms: 15-year maturity, 3 per cent interest. The loan identification number in Kenya's external public debt register is 2016052. This is not a World Bank project and has no P-number.

cases.conditions: The credit paid 85 per cent of the cost of commercial contracts held by a Chinese contractor, China Hydropower International Co., Ltd, with the Kenyan side covering the rest (AidData record 53111). Land acquisition and compensation were the Kenyan state's responsibility, through the National Land Commission.

companies.name: China Hydropower International Co., Ltd (Sinohydro)
companies.role: Contractor for the works the credit financed (AidData record 53111); The Star names Sinohydro Corporation as the firm that built the road

companies.name: Kenya National Highways Authority
companies.role: State roads authority that administered the project (AidData record 53111)
companies.desc: National agency under Kenya's roads ministry responsible for the management, development and maintenance of class A, B and C national trunk roads.

companies.name: National Land Commission
companies.role: The state body that made and then, according to a Senate record, revised downwards the compensation awards (Kenyan Senate Hansard record of Senator Enoch Kiio Wambua)
companies.desc: Independent commission created by Kenya's 2010 constitution to manage public land and to carry out compulsory acquisition and pay compensation under the Land Act.

cases.community: On 6 December 2020 The Star reported that about 5,000 land owners had not been paid for land taken for the tarmacking of the 172 km Kibwezi-Kitui-Migwani road. Their spokesman Michael Kivoto said people had been allocated land by the defunct Kitui County Council and had put up shops and other structures for income, "only for the buildings to be brought down without anyone talking of compensation", that some had gone to court while most could not afford lawyers' fees, and that some of those affected had sunk into depression; a delegation of 26 people took the matter to Kalonzo Musyoka. On 4 March 2022 The Star reported that the project "displaced about 5,000 persons who either lost their land, homes and business premises", that they were asking for Sh1.6 billion and had not been fully compensated five years after work began, and that they demonstrated outside the Kitui county commissioner's office on 3 March 2022. Joseph Wambua said: "We lost property such as houses and farms which were our source of livelihood. Life is tough and the government should stop the delays and pay up." Kanini Kitili said she had lost a big chunk of land and that it was unfair for the government to pay the contractor while no one cared about the displaced. The deputy county commissioner Dorcas Rono said the authorities would follow up the issue. In March 2023 the Member for Kibwezi West, Mwengi Mutuse, asked the Cabinet Secretary for Lands to explain the delay in paying people whose land was compulsorily acquired for the road in 2017 and to say whether the commission would review the compensation upwards given the delay; Parliament's record of the question shows no response. The Star, reporting the question on 21 March 2023, said the commission was to compensate about 5,000 title owners who were relocated for the project and that the families had been pushed out and were wallowing in poverty. A Kenyan Senate record carries Senator Enoch Kiio Wambua saying that officers from the National Land Commission were reviewing awards downwards by a wide margin two months after people had been given an award, that compensation, pollution and the companies' community obligations on this section were all serious, and that he had led a delegation of affected people from Kitui Township to the commission.
cases.displaced_note: The figure of about 5,000 is described three ways in three reports and is not a count of people moved: "about 5,000 land owners" not compensated (The Star, 6 December 2020), "about 5,000 persons who either lost their land, homes and business premises" (The Star, 4 March 2022), and "about 5,000 title owners who were relocated" (The Star, 21 March 2023). No document counting households actually relocated was found.
cases.outcome: The road was completed in May 2022 (The Star, 21 March 2023). The 2023 parliamentary question on the delay has no answer recorded in Parliament's own record of it. No record of payment was found.

cases.confidence_note: The unpaid compensation is carried by a Kenyan newspaper in three reports across 2020, 2022 and 2023, by a parliamentary question whose own record shows no answer, and by a Senate speech, all outside the lender. The figure of about 5,000 comes from that one newspaper and is described differently each time. The Star of 21 March 2023 calls the questioner the Kibwezi East MP while Parliament's record of the question gives the Member for Kibwezi West. The Senate record carried here gives no sitting date, so none is stated. The downward revision of awards rests on that single Senate speech. The amount claimed, Sh1.6 billion, is what those affected asked for, not an assessed figure.
cx: Kibwezi-Mutomo-Kitui road land acquisition and unpaid compensation
cases.whole: The road is part of the Mombasa-Isiolo-Moyale corridor and gives a direct link between Mombasa and Ethiopia; it is used by buses, matatus and trucks heading for Embu, Kiambu, Kitui, Machakos, Makueni, Meru and Mombasa, and cuts at least 100 km off long-distance trips (The Star, 21 March 2023). The project was 53 per cent complete in May 2019 against an original completion date of 15 February 2021, held up by land acquisition, the relocation of power lines along the corridor, late payments, a shortage of water for the works and a stoppage by the contractor after Covid-19 cases in Kitui; residents also complained of noise and dust from the works (AidData record 53111).
